idiom_name: kotlinx.coroutines Channel + N launch{} consumers, CoroutineDispatcher as the performer pool
implementation_notes: kotlinx.coroutines replaces the classic dispatcher with two pieces: a Channel (explicitly documented as conceptually a BlockingQueue with suspending send/receive) is the queue, and usually the fan-out idiom - several coroutines receiving from the same channel - is the performer pool, since the runtime hands each element to exactly one receiver. CoroutineDispatcher decides which thread pool the performers run on (Dispatchers.Default for CPU work, or ExecutorService.asCoroutineDispatcher() when a JVM executor already exists), so the 'pool' is configuration rather than structure. A dedicated dispatcher coroutine is only needed when the assignment must be decided (affinity, per-performer limits); note the documented trap that consumeEach cancels the shared channel, while a plain for-loop is safe to use from several consumers.
pitfalls: consumeEach cancels the underlying channel when it completes, so using it in one of several fan-out consumers tears the channel down for its siblings; iterate with a for-loop instead (documented).
Cancellation is cooperative: a performer that never suspends or checks for cancellation keeps running after its scope is cancelled, delaying shutdown.
channel capacity 0 is a rendezvous - the sender waits for a free performer, so producer throughput becomes coupled to performer availability.
A child coroutine failure cancels the whole scope unless a SupervisorJob separates the performers; use CoroutineExceptionHandler plus a supervisor for message-level isolation.
Blocking calls inside Dispatchers.Default starve the shared pool; use Dispatchers.IO or a dedicated dispatcher for blocking APIs.
